title: The latter glory of this house; the nations' treasures (Hag 2:6–9)
speaker: The LORD through Haggai
description: In a little while the LORD will shake heaven, earth, sea, dry land and all nations; "the precious things of all nations will come", he will fill the house with glory; silver and gold are his; the latter glory of the house will be greater than the former, and in this place he will give peace.
in_text_interpretation: Haggai does not explain the shaking further; 2:21–22 repeats it as the overthrow of kingdoms. Hebrews 12:26–27 applies "once more I will shake" to the removal of created things.

interpretations.label: The Messiah, "the Desire of all nations", would come to the Second Temple (fulfilled in Jesus)
proponents: The Vulgate (et veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus) and older commentators citing Luke 2 (as reported by Mitchell)
D. Guzik (with Trapp): the latter glory greater because the Lord of glory visited it
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: chemdath read as a person ("the desired one"); the glory of the house is the presence of the Messiah. Historical evidence: the Second Temple, enlarged by Herod, stood in Jesus' lifetime. Objection: Mitchell and Keil argue that the parallel "silver … gold" (2:8) shows the word means precious things, not a person.

interpretations.label: The nations' precious things will adorn the rebuilt Temple
proponents: C. F. Keil (1868): the nations coming to the Messiah is foreign to the context
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: chemdath with "silver … gold" (2:8) denotes valuables; Haggai expects the nations, after the coming upheaval, to bring their wealth (cf. Isa 60:5–11). Mitchell holds that Haggai expected this imminently, in the convulsions of Darius's early reign.

interpretations.label: An eschatological shaking of heaven and earth
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: Hebrews quotes 2:6 for a final shaking that leaves only what cannot be shaken. This reading concerns the shaking, not the Temple's glory.
